articles.title: 5 Justice League Unlimited Villains I'm Still Waiting to See on the Big Screen in the DCU
articles.summary: Following the change in leadership, priorities for the DCU and future projects have shifted. David Ellison has expressed an interest in a fast-tracked Justice League, wanting Wonder Woman, Batman, and Aquaman on screens again as soon as possible. Fans have been wanting Batman and Wonder Woman again for years, and putting Aquaman back in the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Following the change in leadership, priorities for the DCU and future projects have shifted . David Ellison has expressed an interest in a fast-tracked Justice League , wanting Wonder Woman, Batman, and Aquaman on screens again as soon as possible. Fans have been wanting Batman and Wonder Woman again for years, and putting Aquaman back in the spotlight makes sense given the financial success of 2018’s Aquaman. With a focus on Justice League stories, there are few better places to look than the largely successful animated series Justice League Unlimited .

While the DCU has already carried over some villains from the show — see Lex Luthor in Superman or Amanda Waller in Creature Commandos — there’s still plenty left to make appearances. With Man of Tomorrow still on track to hit theaters, The People vs. Gorilla Grodd is still expected to introduce audiences to Gorilla Grodd. Gorilla Grodd made appearances in both Justice League and Justice League Unlimited, serving as a mastermind not only behind the Secret Society but also the Legion of Doom. Beyond Luthor and Grodd, DCU villains are still up in the air, but here are five solid picks for the Justice League to battle against.

Done dirty in Wonder Woman ‘84, the archeologist turned demigod Barbara Minerva deserves another shot in the DCU. In the DCAU canon, Barbara Minerva became the Cheetah when funding for her experiments ran out and she started testing on herself. Outcasted as a result, Cheetah turned to a life of crime. In Justice League and Justice League Unlimited , she mainly played a supporting role as one villain amongst a larger ensemble. Cheetah was part of both Lex Luthor’s Injustice Gang and Gorilla Grodd’s Legion of Doom.

Cheetah was largely in the background of episodes, with no strong individual plot of her own. Given the many retcons and alterations to the character , Cheetah could take a variety of forms in the DCU. She could be another monster that was created by experimentation like Matt Hagan in Clayface , or she could help bring in another god through her connection to Urzkartaga.

Darkseid first popped up in the extended animated universe in Superman: The Animated Series , but he's hardly just a Superman villain. He’d make appearances throughout Superman: The Animated Series along with an episode of Justice League prior to his resurrection during the first part of Justice League Unlimited ’s series finale. Due to the magnitude of the threat that Darkseid poses, the Justice League must temporarily ally with Lex Luthor and the Legion of Doom in order to bring Darkseid down.

Darkseid is an easy choice in terms of Justice League level threats, and was set to enter the DCU through the Mister Miracle animated series . With Josh Hutcherson and Mackenzie Davis lending their voices to the show for Mister Miracle and Big Barda, the show seemed well on its way, even though they hadn’t yet cast a voice actor for Darkseid. Given the duo’s ties to Apokolips, the show is a sensible way to introduce him to the DCU, especially since Darkseid has all the makings of a great big bad and would be wasted as a foe in a first or even second Justice League film.

As an evil sorceress from Arthurian times — and the half-sister of King Arthur — Morgaine le Fay had an interesting backstory with the formidable magic powers to match. Unlike the other villains that the Justice League faced throughout Justice League and Justice League Unlimited , Morgaine le Fay didn’t want power for herself, but rather for her son, Mordred. Morgaine le Fay may have only appeared in one episode of Justice League Unlimited, but it was one of the show’s most iconic episodes, and solidified her appearance on this list as a villain the Justice League could face. Magic is a route that hasn’t been explored much in DCU films yet and could make for different feeling films.

The Justice League Unlimited episode “Kid Stuff” saw Morgaine le Fay achieve her goal, but not in the way she intended. Le Fay gets her hands on the Amulet of First Magic which gives her and Mordred enough power to finally conquer the world. Although wanting him to have power, Morgaine le Fay is wary of him using the amulet because he’s too young — an action that causes him to snatch the amulet from her and wish that there were no more adults in the world. All adults are sent to a separate dimension, and Morgaine le Fay offers her services to the Justice League in order to defeat her son. In order to go back to the regular world, Le Fay turns Wonder Woman, Batman, Superman, and Green Lantern into children and wacky cartoon hijinks proceed from there.

2. Felix Faust More than just a tad pathetic, Faust is arguably one of the most memorable villains of the Justice League cartoons. Having made a Faustian bargain, Faust’s evil deeds are often in service of a higher power, such as Hades, putting him in direct conflict with Diana. Felix Faust very much felt like her villain, especially given the damage he did to Themyscira in “Paradise Lost”. Faust, under the tutelage of Hades, knew what Diana’s vulnerable spots were — her mother and sisters — and used them against her in order to get what he wanted. Unlike other heroes and their antagonists, the confrontation between Diana and Felix Faust had real consequences. Although acting in the island’s best interest, Diana’s choice to bring in the rest of the Justice League gets her exiled because she broke the “no men” rule that the island upheld.

The other Felix Faust story “The Balance” sees Diana returning to Themyscira once again in the aftermath of Felix Faust usurping Hades’s throne in Tartarus. Diana and Hawkgirl free Hades from his torment and together the three stop Faust. In the end, Diana’s welcomed back to Themyscria and Hades tasks himself with looking after the sole piece of Faust’s soul left. In the comics, Faust is frequently up to no good, often posing as other beings such as Dr. Fate and Deadman in order to achieve his ends. Faust could then be a compelling villain for the DCU and add complicated layers to what could otherwise be a straightforward story.

Brainiac is the type of villain that feels closer to a when, than an if, he’ll appear in the DCU. Although closely tied to Superman, Brainiac is a threat large enough to demand the attention of the whole Justice League. The Kryptonian AI — him originating from Krypton was a change made for Superman: The Animated Series in order to tie him closer to the Man of Steel  — continued his usual quest to destroy sources of knowledge after he attained the most valuable bits, putting him in direct conflict with the Man of Steel. 

Justice League Unlimited saw the character literally fuse with Lex Luthor becoming a hybrid of the two villains. Brainiac admits his role in curing Luthor’s kryptonite-induced cancer, showing just the tip of the iceberg of Brainiac’s power. Brainiac is presumed destroyed following Flash forcibly separating the two, but Gorilla Grodd reveals that he managed to save a fragment. Luthor then spends much of the third season of Unlimited obsessed with trying to merge with Brainiac again. Ultimately, Luthor fails in his quest and it is his unending efforts that bring forth Darkseid instead. Bringing Brainiac into the DCU is a no-brainer in terms of giving not only Superman another big bad, but also expands the universe given Brainiac’s plethora of knowledge and abilities. 

Which Justice League Unlimited villain are you still waiting for? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: Tim Burton’s Batman Plans Included a Radical Idea for Robin, And Toys Were Made Before It Was Scrapped
articles.summary: When Michael Keaton was cast as Batman in Tim Burton's 1989 film, everybody was shocked by the choice. Years later, many continue to say how great his performance was and place him high among the best actors to wear the cowl. Controversial casting choices are plentiful in comic book to movie adaptations, but there was […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google When Michael Keaton was cast as Batman in Tim Burton's 1989 film, everybody was shocked by the choice. Years later, many continue to say how great his performance was and place him high among the best actors to wear the cowl. Controversial casting choices are plentiful in comic book to movie adaptations, but there was one in this legendary DC franchise that would have shook the fandom to its core if it actually happened. Burton had the revolutionary idea of recasting Dick Grayson/ Robin as a Black character and felt that the perfect face for the iconic domino mask was Marlon Wayans.

The story behind this casting choice and what happened after a deal was reached is wild, and feels like it came straight out of a comic instead of real life. We all know that Wayans was never formally part of the franchise, but if rumor and innuendo are to be believed, he actually left a permanent mark on Batman that was a part of the childhood of many 90's kids and we didn't even know it. Even though Burton's unique proposal for Robin never made it into movie theaters, it may have made its way into the hand of any children who played with Batman action figures.

Tim Burton's Batman movie became one of the highest-grossing movies of 1989, making a sequel inevitable. There were a few things Burton wanted to accomplish in his first film that he tried to add into this second entry, including the introduction of Batman's sidekick, Robin. The character was removed from earlier drafts of the script since the producers felt there were too many characters already and not enough time to introduce The Boy Wonder, so Robin was sidelined until Batman Returns was in the works.

Meanwhile, Marlon Wayans was a newcomer to Hollywood , making his cinematic debut in his older brother Keenan's parody of 70's blaxploitation flicks, I'm Gonna Git You Sucka . His family had some star power attached to their names, but Marlon was a relative unknown at the time, and this anonymity appealed to Burton. The plan was to have Grayson be introduced in the sequel as himself, making a cameo as a mechanic who fixes the Batmobile. If a third film was made, Wayans would return and officially pick up the mantle as Robin.

Once again, Grayson was cut from Batman Returns due to the number of new characters introduced in the sequel. Despite this removal, Wayans was signed to be a part of the third movie in 1995, Batman Forever , but Tim Burton was ousted in favor of Joel Schumacher with the hopes that the picture would be less grim and easier to merchandise. As the film shifted in a different direction, Wayans was dropped and replaced by Chris O'Donnell. Luckily for Marlon, he was still paid for his nonappearance as the character and continues to receive royalties to this day for a movie he was never in. It doesn't completely remove the sting Wayans felt from losing out on this role, but it certainly helps the actor whose perspective on it has viewed the entire scenario in a more positive light.

"If Robin happened, I wouldn't be Marlon," the youngest sibling of the Wayans family explained during an interview with People Magazine earlier this year. "I might've blown up and become something different. I might've been Will Smith, but then I wouldn't be Marlon… Everything in my life has happened for a reason, and you may not understand it in the moment, but now that I'm 53, I can look back at that disappointed 19-year-old who got that part and was so hurt that it didn't happen, and I'm  glad  it didn't happen."

Officially and canonically, Marlon Wayans was never Robin in an onscreen role. However, many signs point to his version of the character being immortalized in plastic as an action figure. Production had already moved forward for toy manufacturer Kenner, who made the previous film's figures and were hard at work preparing for a new wave to coincide with the release of Batman Returns . According to the legends about this figure, Kenner didn't get the memo about Robin being cut from the script until it was too late. Instead, they continued working on the toys and allegedly repainted the product to a different skintone while keeping the sculpt unchanged.

Those who believe this theory point out the flat-top on Robin's head, which would make more sense for a Black character to have than a White one. However, some believe this was Kenner's interpretation of Norm Breyfogle's work on the character from the ongoing Batman comics or Tom Lyle's artwork from his 1991 Robin solo mini-series. Looking at the illustrations from both artists, the figure certainly shares inspiration from those appearances but the figure's hair is visibly taller and shaped differently than what Tim Drake typically had. No amount of gel would give Drake that kind of height, so there is likely some credence to this belief about Wayans being the basis of the toy.

Unfortunately, there has never been concrete evidence to separate what is fact from fiction, and this could be a case of inspiration coming from both the comic and movie sides. Fast forward to more recent events in the Batman '89 comic from 2021, and a character named Winston Drake debuted and went on to become Robin, fulfilling one of Burton's plans that never happened in the movies. As far as eight-year-old me is concerned, I'm still grateful that I had such a cool Robin figure to play with, and I appreciate the fact that whether it is or isn't Marlon Wayans, that guy had some real smarts to get paid for a role he never actually performed.

Would Marlon Wayans' career have been changed for the better or worse if he played Robin in a Batman movie? Join the conversation in the comments below and let us know how you feel about this decision.

articles.content:
The BBC has been told that its £500 million ($655M) savings plan will have a bigger impact on audiences than previous cuts, according to a new report.

The UK's National Audit Office (NAO) spending watchdog warned that the £500M target is a "significant step up" in savings efforts and will likely "result in more noticeable changes for audiences."

The BBC has been steadily announcing cuts in recent months, including plans to slash 2,000 jobs, close services like BBC Three, and cancel shows such as RuPaul's Drag Race UK . Related Stories News BBC Deputy Boss Questions Impact Of "Creative Choices Taken On West Coast Of United States" On UK Audiences News Melissa George Leading BBC-BritBox Detective Series 'The Loch Ness Mysteries'

The BBC has unveiled roughly £200M of the savings , which are required because the broadcaster has hemorrhaged more than two million licence fee payers since 2020. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

In a 52-page report, the NAO said: "Larger savings from scope reductions, delivered at a faster pace, could increase the risk of cumulative impacts on audiences, reputation and services, while potentially reducing the BBC’s capacity to manage further change."

The NAO warned that layoffs at the BBC could mean a brain drain that increases the risk of mistakes in content. In compiling the report, the BBC told the NAO that errors — such as Gaza: How to Survive a Warzone being narrated by the child of a Hamas minister — were not related to cuts.

The BBC acknowledged, however, that there is a "risk that further headcount reductions could result in the loss of staff with important skills and long-term experience of maintaining editorial integrity."

The NAO added: "The BBC’s efforts to achieve savings could reduce its data and cyber capability; delay investment in replacing ageing technology; and increase dependence on third-party suppliers."

The spending watchdog said the BBC should review whether its governance arrangements for delivering savings remain appropriate for the £500M plan.

articles.title: 5 Sci-Fi Movies That Were Too Ambitious For Their Own Good, Including Multiple Directors’ Pet Projects
articles.summary: The science fiction genre is one of the most consistently successful and popular in modern cinema, and each passing year offers exciting new releases. It's no secret that sci-fi sells, as some of the most iconic movie franchises are those that incorporate elements of science fiction into their stories. Many of the best sci-fi movies […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The science fiction genre is one of the most consistently successful and popular in modern cinema, and each passing year offers exciting new releases. It's no secret that sci-fi sells, as some of the most iconic movie franchises are those that incorporate elements of science fiction into their stories. Many of the best sci-fi movies are those that take place in awe-inspiring settings, imagining futuristic or mind-bending settings and scenarios for their stories to unfold in. In many ways, modern science fiction is as much about interesting concepts as it is about the execution, and sci-fi movies always seem to strive to deliver more of what fans seem to want.

Recently, we looked at fantasy movies that were too ambitious for their own good , and it turns out there are many sci-fi movies that fit the same profile. In their attempts to establish and deliver sprawling, compelling worlds filled with original ideas and unique characters, the following movies seemed to lose something that was far more important. Quantity should never outweigh quality, but that's something that these sci-fi movies all struggled with, and it ultimately backfired in pretty spectacular fashion.

Unfortunately, Jupiter Ascending is remembered mostly as a sci-fi movie so bad it's actually good , despite being the product of the minds behind The Matrix . The Wachowskis' attempt to deliver a completely original space opera fell short of expectations, although not necessarily for the reasons that seem obvious upon watching the movie. Admittedly, its lack of quality leaves a lot to be desired, but the reason the movie struggles is simply because it tries to do far too much all at once.

Introducing an elaborate galactic hierarchy of interplanetary politics, ancient alien dynasties, and an assortment of other sci-fi ideas all in a single movie saw Jupiter Ascending go from a movie with promise to a jumbled mess. Clearly intended to serve as the first chapter of an epic new space opera franchise, Jupiter Ascending instead fell flat, because the sheer amount of exposition required to make its story work made even its most promising elements collapse. In simple terms, the worldbuilding completely overwhelmed the narrative, and so much attention was given to establishing the bigger picture that the movie just wasn't very good on its own individual merit.

There aren't too many sci-fi movies that are terrible from beginning to end , but Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets is one of them. Remembered as the vanity project of the legendary sci-fi director Luc Besson, Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets served as an adaptation of the French comic book series Valérian and Laureline . In fairness to both Besson and the movie, in a visual sense it's both impressive and imaginative, although by almost every other conceivable metric, it's borderline unwatchable.

Filmmakers getting to realize their pet projects often leads to great things, but huge-budget sci-fi is always a risk, and Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets proves why. The priority seemed to be delivering an elaborate sci-fi world rather than telling an engaging story, and the total lack of chemistry between its stars, Dane DeHaan and Cara Delevingne, certainly didn't help. Had the movie been developed as a smaller-scale, more cohesive story first and a worldbuilding exercise second, it might have stood a chance, but ultimately, Besson's vision was far too ambitious for the movie to pull off.

Creating an ambitious sci-fi movie isn't always a case of bringing a fantastical world to life. 2004's Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow is remembered as a great sci-fi movie that continues to boast a cult following, but that doesn't mean that its ambitious nature didn't backfire. Starring Jude Law, Angelina Jolie, and Gwyneth Paltrow, the core idea behind the movie was to create a film that felt like a living illustration to serve as a love letter to the sci-fi serials and pulp magazines of the 1930s. Shot using an almost entirely digital environment, Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow is a film that largely lived up to the ambition behind it.

However, just because the movie achieved its goal and earned critical success, that doesn't mean its ambitious nature didn't backfire. General audiences found the visual style a little jarring, and many rejected the groundbreaking idea as a result. For all the ways that the experimental filmmaking technique made Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow stand out as a truly unique sci-fi film, it also alienated the wider audience that would have secured its success. The ambition behind the movie was, and remains to this day, commendable, but it ironically led to the movie struggling to achieve the recognition it deserved.

Across the genre's history, there have been a few painfully slow sci-fi movies that deserved to be much better than they were. 2012's Cloud Atlas is perhaps a prime example of this phenomenon, as the very notion of adapting David Mitchell's sci-fi novel onto the big screen was a more ambitious undertaking than most filmmakers would even want to consider. However, Tom Tykwer and the Wachowskis (yes, them again) sought to do just that, and the result is perhaps one of the purest examples of a movie too ambitious for its own good.

In order to explain why Cloud Atlas was such an ambitious adaptation, we need only to look at its story. Telling six stories across six different periods of human history, Cloud Atlas jumps between eras, making various complex links between its many characters. This not only led to its bloated three-hour runtime, but to a film that struggles to make any of its individual stories feel especially worthwhile. The overall product certainly isn't bad, and Cloud Atlas is considered a very rewarding watch by some, but the simple fact remains that turning Mitchell's novel into a big-budget sci-fi movie was an idea that was far too ambitious to ever really pull off.

Once upon a time, Zack Snyder was tipped to direct his own Star Wars movie. When the project fell through, Snyder opted instead to adapt his ideas into a space opera franchise of his own, and the result was Rebel Moon . Considering the way it came about, we can move past the derivative nature of its story, but what is particularly hard to reconcile is how overly ambitious Snyder was in his vision for the film. It's impossible to deny that Rebel Moon 's first chapter had both style and promise in spades, and it introduced many compelling characters that set up a sci-fi franchise worth getting excited for.

The problem with Rebel Moon - Part One: A Child of Fire is that it felt like a sci-fi movie trying too hard to be the next Star Wars . The first film had heaps of promise, but it felt like only part of a story, because so much time and attention was given to setting up the franchise that the film itself didn't really have a full plot. The sheer ambition of Rebel Moon is worth commending, because it epitomises Snyder's strengths as a filmmaker: it's sleek, eye-catching, and action-packed. However, in its attempts to set up a world which, admittedly, is incredibly engaging, the first film ironically ruined the franchise's chances for success by neglecting its own individual story.

EXCLUSIVE: Vertical video streamer Epis is readying a pair of true crime originals, The Swindler and the Billionaire Murder and Two Marys .

Epis is framing the series as "premium true crime" and claims this is the first a microdrama-style service has created something in this vein.

Both shows come from Fremantle's Silvio Productions, which co-produces Netflix true crime shows Death of the Pastor’s Wife , which hit No. 1 on the streamer's global English TV chart for two weeks, and Cold Case: The Tylenol Murders , which reached No. 2 and ranked in the weekly Top 10 across 84 countries. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News BBC And Channel 4 Shows Repurposed For RoseBerry Media's New Vertical Video Service Epis News 'Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' 2nd Best Franchise Previews With $21M+; Scorches 'Wicked' & 'The Odyssey' - Box Office

The Swindler and the Billionaire Murder looks at the death of billionaire banker Edmond Safra in a Monaco fire and the story of his nurse, Ted Maher, as three women pursue the truth over decades. Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

Two Marys delves into the story of women with the same name who are murdered in the same city just days apart. Twenty-five years later, their daughters revisit the cases and the possibility of mistaken identity.

Premiere dates will be announced at a later date, with both series exclusive to Epis, which is part of the U.S.-headquartered RoseBerry Media.

Yotam Guendelman, CEO and director of Silvio, praised Epis CEO Guy Hameiri and his team, "who gave us the time and money to treat this project the same way we treat TV shows," adding: "I know that's not usually the case in the vertical space."

"Our mission is to show there’s an audience for vertical television beyond microdrama," said RoseBerry co-founder and boss Hameiri in an interview with Deadline. "True crime has a huge following, and the way an investigation unfolds lends itself to short episodes. In a cold case, one witness’s account can change how you understand a piece of evidence.

"We’re building RoseBerry as a home for world-class producers who want to help define premium vertical television. Yotam and the team at Silvio have had a remarkable run on Netflix, and their series Buried earned two Emmy nominations. With Two Marys and The Swindler and the Billionaire Murder , we wanted Yotam to bring that same documentary craft to stories told in short chapters.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Guendelman added: “I can't say I'd watched any micro-dramas before doing this – and honestly, not many since – so when Guy approached me about financing a true crime doc as a vertical show, my response was more of a 'why not?'

"I guess the trashy reputation of the micro-drama world makes people ask, 'Why would you work in that space?' Maybe if I watched those shows I'd feel the same. But in my mind, the culture and the zeitgeist have lived on our phones for a very long time, so it's actually surprising we're only making these shows now."

As to why a true crime vertical appealed, Guendelman said: "Real life is the language of social media, so people are already used to watching a kind of documentary on their phones without even realizing it. True crime, with its mystery, pace and twists, has the rhythm you need to compete for attention, but my guess is that any genre can work if the story is compelling enough. The economics are still a bit unknown, but I think we'll find out in the next few months whether this can be a viable, thriving format."

Since launch this year, Epis has built out a true crime slate of more than 75 titles and 2,250 short-form episodes repurposed from their original longer-form format and sourced from the likes of Fremantle, Banijay Rights, All3Media International, Cineflix Rights, Farpoint Films and Woodcut Media. These include Surviving Ted Bundy , Surviving Jeffrey Dahmer , My Twisted Half , Charmed to Death , Forgive Me Captain For I Have Sinned , Lost from Memory and Where Are You, Kathleen?,

There have been debates breaking out around microdrama distribution, with some stars understood to be unhappy with their TV series being repurposed for the medium. However, that's less likely to happen with unscripted and true crime, allowing Epis to quickly build up a slate.

Hameiri said conversations with distributors had developed when the sellers began exploring what new opportunities their library titles had and what value there was to unlock.

"It reminds me of the early days of cable TV," he added. "Rights owners could license a programme to a new channel, reach new audiences, and earn more from a title they’d already invested in. At Roseberry, we believe vertical TV can do something similar. A distributor with a strong true-crime catalogue can bring those stories to audiences watching on their phones. That’s the massive opportunity we see and are hearing from our partners and rights owners.”

articles.title: 4 Years Ago, Star Wars TV's Best Series Delivered an Action Scene That Rivaled the Movies
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Comics Star Wars is in a very strange place in 2026. The franchise has been under Disney ownership for over a decade and the best way to describe the reception is mixed. The sequel trilogy has its fans, but it also has its naysayers. Rogue One was a hit with fans, but Solo wasn't. The shows […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Star Wars is in a very strange place in 2026. The franchise has been under Disney ownership for over a decade and the best way to describe the reception is mixed. The sequel trilogy has its fans, but it also has its naysayers. Rogue One was a hit with fans, but Solo wasn't. The shows have run of the gamut of being beloved like The Mandalorian , being hated like The Acolyte , and no one ever talking about them, like Skeleton Crew . However, there is a Star Wars show that is both loved by fans and critics alike – Andor . This show is one of the best pieces of Star Wars media ever , if not the greatest, and four years ago it proved it by giving us one of the coolest action scenes ever, one that rivaled the movies.

The first season of Andor was something of a revelation for fans. The varying quality of Star Wars media (I was going to type "in the Disney era", but let's be real – the quality of Star Wars has always been all over the place) meant that no one really knew what kind of show we were going to get before it started. The show impressed right away and it did it by being both the most Star Wars thing ever and also completely different from another Star War (take some money to go see one). However, the penultimate episode included an action scene that was pure Star Wars , rivaling anything fans had seen on the big screen.

Before Andor , Star Wars media was basically just adventure stories. Sure, there were deeper themes to the whole thing, but for the most part, it was just a modernization of the adventure serials that George Lucas watched a child. While the franchise played with fascism, rebellion, spirituality, family dynamics, and the like, it was first and foremost an exciting war in the stars (well, when it all worked out). Andor was originally very different from what we got , but the show was never going to be typical Star Wars .

I'm going to take a second out to define "typical Star Wars ", so we all know where I'm starting from. Star Wars typically is grandiose battles between good and evil, defined by the lightsaber fights that are metaphors for the clashing of opposing ideologies and massive space battle scenes. When it all works right, these types of action scenes are cathartic moments in the narrative, their pulse-pounding action bringing the stories to their culmination.

Andor was very short on typical Star Wars . While the show opened with Andor killing someone while looking for his sister, it wasn't the kind of exciting Star Wars scene we were used to; it was something out of a spy thrilller or a crime movie. I've experienced a lot of types of Star Wars stories over the decades – I was an avid EU readers up until the Disney purchase – and Andor was very much unique in the annals of the franchise, especially for fans who never ventured past the movies (if you want something amazing that isn't even close to canon anymore, look for "Interlude at Darkknell" for the best finding the Death Star plans story ever).

It was the definition of a slow burn, which is one of the reasons the scene where Luthen escapes the Cantwell -class's tractor beams (using a modification on the EU cloak shroud gambit; some of you know what I'm talking about, the rest of you should run to Google or your AI friend and find out) works so well. This scene was typical Star Wars , but it was also one of the only times in the entire first season that we got a scene like this.

One of the complaints you saw a lot during Andor Season One was that it was too slow. Some of those watching it wanted something more akin to the excitement of Rogue One instead of what was more a somber meditation of the effects of fascism on a society. One of the things I've always found so interesting about Star Wars fans is that there are some of them who want the franchise to go all kinds of different directions and there are some who just want lightsabers and starfighters. And here's the thing – the producers of the franchise know that.

There's a world where someone higher up at LucasFilm or Disney stepped in and told Tony Gilroy that he needed to add Darth Vader and about four outer space action scenes. However, they trusted him and let him tell the story his way, leading up to this scene. This is the scene that even the most unabashed Andor haters love because it is everything that you expect from a big space action scene in Star Wars . It reminded people that this was still the galaxy far, far away. It was also was one of the most unique scenes in the show.

There's also a world where the producers demanded this scene was put somewhere closer to the beginning, in order to give viewers that comfortable Star Wars feeling. Thank the Force (which is female, haters) that we didn't get there, because the main reason this scene works so well is this series wasn't typical Star Wars . It was something of a surprise to get a scene like this (as a ship geek, I love the Cantwell ; Imperial design philosophy just does it for me) in the show and that was part of made it work so well. We didn't know what to expect at the beginning of the show; Gilroy and company did a fantastic job of establishing how different Andor was, but this scene reminded us that it was still Star Wars .

Andor has a lot in common with The Acolyte. Both of them are rather well made shows and both of them have a devoted section of the fanbase that hates them with a burning passion (I wouldn't be surprised if they were the same people; Acolyte haters are the kind of people who actually like fascism). Both of them went in different directions than we're used to with their stories and each of them had scenes toward the end that would have made the naysayers happier if they had happened earlier, but would have damaged the show immensely.

Andor was an anti-fascist polemic disguised in Star Wars clothing and that outfit wouldn't be complete without this scene. It was the moment that reminded you that the war against the Empire was, well, a war, one where the smaller side had to use ingenuity to defeat their all-powerful enemies. In a lot of ways, it's the story of Andor in microcosm. Much like the Fondor Haulcraft, the characters of the show have hidden depths and often devastating tricks. While they can't destroy their enemy outright, they can hurt them, turning their own weapons against them. By holding this scene of traditional Star Wars action to the end, Andor 's producers were able to make their show even better, perfectly building to this moment (and, of course, the final episode's amazing funeral scene on Ferrix, a less Star Wars -like action scene that is all the better because this scene preceded it).

What do you think about the fight between Luthen's Haulcraft and the Cantwell ? Is it your favorite Star Wars space action scene or is it the Battle of Ebaq 9 (some of you know, others are Googling)? Sound off in the comment section below.

articles.title: "Learn From the Mistakes of Mentors": The Head of Tallinn's Discovery Campus Is All About Bridging Film Education and Industry
articles.summary: Sri Lankan cinematographer Dhanushka Gunathilake took over the talent and industry platform of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival's Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event this year. And he has ambitious plans.
articles.content:
Seven years ago, Sri Lankan cinematographer Dhanushka Gunathilake ( Between Yesterday and Tomorrow , Dark in the White Light ) and his family moved to the capital of Estonia because his wife got a chance to study at Tallinn University.

The creative, whose film The Frozen Fire was Sri Lanka’s first-ever submission for the best international feature film Oscar, soon got involved with the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), whose 30th edition wraps up this weekend, and its Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event (ITBE) market. At PÖFF, he worked as a TV host, Q&A moderator and project manager at the talent and industry platform Discovery Campus, where he spearheaded Frame Within a Frame, the fest’s cinematography-dedicated masterclass initiative. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies "I'm in Preparation for the End of Our World": Golshifteh Farahani on Art, War and Her Tallinn Premiere Movies IDFA: 'The Year of the Ghost' and 'Memories of Lightning' Win Amsterdam Doc Fest Awards

This year, he took over as the head of the Discovery Campus. In between his busy schedule, Gunathilake caught up with THR to share his vision for the platform and why it is such a key part of the Tallinn sucess formula.

Each year, the Discovery Campus welcomes around 70 emerging professionals and talents, from producers and directors to cinematographers, production designers, composers and production designers, to its workshops and masterclasses.

Gunathilake says it is all about building bridges. And that goes beyond the bridges and networks that socializing and discussing the craft naturally creates. "There is a gap between academia and the film industry," he tells THR . "We thought it is a responsibility of film festivals to help bridge industry and academia and bring them together."

Case in point: Students fresh out of film schools, whether focused on cinematography or other areas, "may have never heard of a sales agent and what they do, they don't know what distribution is and they have never heard of a subject called audience study," he explains. "So we thought it would be very interesting to introduce this ecosystem of the afterlife of the film when they make one? What actually happens to this film?" blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Gunathilake says beyond general education, mentorship is a key focus for him and his team. "It is important to create a platform where mentors are coming – big filmmakers – and emerging talents can present their film and have an exchange with them. They can come together and sit and talk and discuss."

The feedback on these opportunities is strong to enthusiastic. For example, one younger cinematographer from Spain got to spend time with the acclaimed Roberto Schaefer ( Finding Neverland , Monster's Ball , Quantum of Solace ). "She mentioned that she never thought she could sit at a breakfast table and talk about her film with Roberto," Gunathilake tells THR . "And Roberto had seen her film, and then they could talk."

The importance of mentoring is actually captured in the official motto of the Discovery Campus that is featured on its website: "Learn from the mistakes of our mentors, so you don’t have to make them yourself!"

Among the big industry names who have shared their insights and tips at Tallinn this year are the likes of Sentimental Value casting director Yngvill Haga , Julio Macat, the cinematographer behind the likes of Miracle on 34th Street and Home Alone , and dual screenplay Oscar winner Christopher Hampton .

The Discovery Campus head's ambitions don't stop here, though. "We already have a plan for the next five years," he shares. "We plan to expand into a year-long program soon. And our ultimate target is to build a talent bank. For example, if any director, producer, or any filmmaker wants to hunt for emerging talents, this should be the platform that they use." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Indian-Australian filmmaker Anoop Lokkur , whose debut "Don't Tell Mother" premiered at the Busan International Film Festival in 2025, is turning his own standoff with tenants who wouldn't leave his family home into "Melgade Mane Kelgade Mane" (Upstairs Downstairs), a dark comedy in the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar .

The Kannada and English-language film follows Karthik, who returns from Melbourne, along with his wife and young daughter, to look after his ailing father. He expects to take over the top floor of the house in an older Bengaluru neighborhood where his family has lived for three generations. The tenant, government contractor Ramesh, had agreed to move out, then changes his mind. Lokkur says that in 2025 he returned to Bangalore with his wife and their 1-year-old daughter, planning to settle upstairs in his parents' home, but the tenants stayed on after their lease ran out and the family ended up crammed into his parents' part of the house. "The whole situation was frustrating and unpleasant. What followed were months of tension, passive aggression and even thinking of ways to get them to vacate. The irony, though, was that only a couple of years earlier, my wife and I had been forced out of a rented home ourselves."

Having been on both sides of the door, he says, he grew curious about ownership, about what it means to call a place home and about how hard people will push to come out on top. The project is in development, with Lokkur and Mikayla Henke producing through Papunu Films. The budget is $1.3 million, with $156,000 in place, and the team is looking for international co-producers, financiers and sales agents in Goa.

"The film is built like a tennis match. Your sympathies keep switching between the two families, until you're no longer sure who to cheer for," Lokkur says. "I'm interested in how ego quietly takes over and how ordinary decent people justify each small act of revenge until they no longer recognize themselves. It's also a film about Bangalore, a city changing so fast that old neighborhoods and family homes are disappearing."

Henke says she went through the dispute alongside Lokkur, and that with the family living it every day, it was the obvious choice for their next film. "'Don't Tell Mother' was a tender and very personal film. On the surface, 'Melgade Mane Kelgade Mane' (Upstairs Downstairs) might look like the opposite: darker, bolder and funnier. But it comes from the same place, a close eye on family and the things people struggle to say to each other. This time, we just want to take audiences on a much wilder ride."

"Don't Tell Mother" played in the A Window on Asian Cinema section at Busan, was nominated for best youth film at the 2026 Asia Pacific Screen Awards and had its Australian premiere at this year's Sydney Film Festival. Lokkur's short "Long Distance," which Henke produced, screened at the Melbourne International Film Festival and Palm Springs International ShortFest before Canal+ acquired it. Henke was also the first producer on "Don't Tell Mother."

"While it's set in Bengaluru, it's a universal story about housing that people everywhere can relate to and we believe it can travel well beyond India," the producers say.

WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

We can reveal Sarinah Masukor, co-writer of Netflix miniseries My Brilliant Career , and Keir Wilkins ( Heartbreak High ) have been brought on as writers for Season 2, which is currently in development at SBS under lead writer and co-creator Elise McCredie.

Wooden Horse co-founder Richard Finlayson confirmed the show is in the works, telling Deadline: "We’re developing a second series with SBS, and the writers are back in the room under Elise McCready’s guidance."

Jude Troy, who launched the Sydney-based Wooden Horse with Finlayson, co-created the show with McCredie. Weaving stars alongside The Pitt breakout Shabana Azeez, Claudia Karvan ( Bump ), Thomas Weatherall ( Heartbreak High ) and Erroll Shand ( All Her Fault ).

The news came in an exclusive interview during which Wooden Horse's bosses also revealed a host of hires, and projects such as the first Australian adaptation of an R.L. Stein book as a TV series, along with co-production developments with the likes of I May Destroy You and Two Weeks in August maker Various Artists Limited and Wild Cards producer. "We have a great team and a lot of different international relationships and collaborations underway," said Finlayson.

The Airport Chaplain has been a breakout hit for Australian multicultural public service broadcaster SBS, achieving its biggest launch of 2026 with 1.7 million tuning in for episode one and streaming records broken. Netflix took worldwide rights, as we revealed , and its safe to say it has been one of the most notable new series out of Australia this year.

The eight-part show stars Weaving as as unconventional airport terminal chaplain Tobias Wallace and The Pitt breakout Shabana Azeez as his put-upon boss. The show was inspired by Troy's chance encounter with a Melbourne Airport chaplain, who helped her recover a lost handbag.

Troy pointed to the show's "rounded realism," and noted it "takes some big swings in the stories it deals with, but it does so with a light touch and real humanity," noting that there have been "great responses" from viewers in the U.S., UK and her home country, Ireland, among other territories.

"It speaks to humanity and connects with people," said Troy. "Audiences today are looking for something like that. It is a world and a precinct we all recognise, that we have all travelled through, and it depicts very real people doing very real jobs.

"It is about the lower echelons of the airport and the clash with the upper echelons, and shows a working-class perspective that you don’t often see on Australian television."

Former ABC television chief Finlayson and ex-eOne TV production chief Troy co-founded Wooden Horse with Troy in 2020, as we revealed at the time , and have over the following six years established the company among the leaders in Australia. In a tough market where even the likes of NBCUniversal-backed Matchbox Pictures closed down this year, that's no mean feat.

"We are six years in, and I think we have developed a brand that is known for interesting approaches and stories, strong relationships with the best creators and being a trusted producer," said Finlayson. "Now it is about having the capacity to keep delivering, because we have a lot in development and a number going into production."

Credits include the Logie-winning ABC scripted shows The Clearing and Mother and Son , unscripted series Stuff the British Stole , which is being developed as a TV drama, and Deep North true crime doc series The Cape , and there's about to be a flood of new work hitting the market.

Upcoming is a first children's TV show, live-action drama Emma's Dance Club , which is also noteworthy for its combined TV and movie theater rollout. "The first season has 20 episodes, and we have created five packages, each effectively an hour long," said Finlayson. "Hoyts will release them over the course of the year as family experiences. Hoyts has a large family loyalty club, so it is an interesting way to bring together different release strategies."

We can reveal Wooden Horse has teamed with U.S.-based producer Global Production Studios (GPS) on a screen adaptation of spooky YA stories author R.L. Stine's Dangerous Girls , with Thomas Wilson-White, who wrote episodes of Netflix's Heartbreak High , helming the project.

"This is the first time R.L. Stine has ever been adapted in Australia," said Troy.

She also noted there Wooden Horse has an unnamed co-production with Canada's Blink49 Studios underway, while the heist caper adaptation of Australian unscripted series Stuff the British Stole is now known as Plunder and has UK producer Various Artists Limited aboard, along with Warner Bros. International Television Production Australia, as we revealed in June 2024.

Anchuli Felicia King, who wrote on HBO’s The Sympathizer and The Baby and Deadloch for Prime Video, is the writer and creator. Elsewhere, an adaptation of Ashley Collins' Dark Mode with Dan March's Dynamic Television, announced in January 2025, is being set up with an unnamed commissioner, with Safe Home writer Anna Barnes attached. There's also work ongoing to finance The Other Guy star and creator Matt Okine's debut feature film in Queensland. We first flagged development on Being Black n’ Chicken n’ Chips when Wooden Horse launched six years ago.

Wooden Horse has backed up a busy 2026 with series of hires, which we can officially reveal here. Felicity Harrison has joined as the producer's first Head of Commercial and Business Affairs.

She was business affairs chief at Matchbox, which shuttered in February after 18 years in business. At Wooden Horse, she will focus on areas such as legal, business affairs and growing revenues. "We've benefitted from Matchbox's misfortune, as they had such a great team of people," said Finlayson.

Bridget Harvey has become Senior Development Executive, joining from Mr Inbetween and Sunny Nights maker Jungle, and Alexis Talbot Smith ( The Familiars ) joined as a development producer in charge after spells at WildBear and Aquarius Films, with her first job being an associate producer on Emma's Dance Club , on which she led the day-to-day work.

Production and development assistant and coordinator Will Lane has been promoted and Nell O'Grady has been hired from Stranger Than Fiction Films in a similar role. The Other Guy star Okine remains within the company as an exec producer.

Staffing up has been a key part of forward planning for what's gearing up to be a big 2027 for company, which is operating in an Australian creative market that has appeared on the up for several years now.

Finlayson gave a measured assessment of the production sector, noting the strength of local commissioners, who include such as the ABC, SBS, Stan, Binge and Network Seven, and investment from global streamer, who have continued to order originals under the quota system introduced in late 2025 .

"We are well supported by our broadcasters and by local and global streamers, the public broadcasters are relatively well funded, and the Labour government has been supportive. The quotas make a difference, so the local market is in a pretty good place.

"The challenges for Australian producers are much the same as those facing British producers. The U.S. market has changed structurally and is still in a state of flux. We are not seeing it return to pre-COVID levels, so raising the gap is hard for everyone. You have to be well networked internationally and agile when it comes to working with budgets."

Troy addressed how to remain independent in a global production landscape where Banijay Entertainment is now the largest studio outside of the Hollywood big guns, and M&A appears only to apply to those seeking mega-scale. Wooden Horse is owned by its founders, and has investors and board members including Damian Keogh, CEO of theater chain Hoyts, and Peter Allen, former CEO of Scentre Group and current Chairman of Coles.

"There are always conversations, and the rumour mill is always active," she said. "Fully independent Australian companies have shown how agile they can be. That flexibility matters. Not being tethered to one mothership is probably how we have continued to get projects made."
